articles.title: From Natalie Harp to a mysterious object in space: 5 strange US stories you may have missed
articles.summary: US News: From an obscure White House aide suddenly becoming a national obsession to a mysterious kidney disease appearing among Texas farm workers, the first h.
articles.body: From an obscure White House aide suddenly becoming a national obsession to a mysterious kidney disease appearing among Texas farm workers, the first half of September has produced a peculiar collection of American stories. Some are political, some deeply cultural and some almost absurd on the surface.1. Natalie Harp, Aaron Rupar and what made White House angryNatalie Harp, the 35-year-old White House executive assistant, has spent months attracting attention because of her unusually close working relationship with Donald Trump. But in September, the story acquired a new chapter: a $45,000 cash gift disclosed by Harp, followed days later by an extraordinary White House attack on journalist Aaron Rupar after he pointed out that Harp was travelling with Trump in Ireland.Natalie Harp is called the human printer as she carries a portable printer and battery pack, allowing her to give Trump physical copies of news articles and social-media material.The controversy took a financial turn after it was reported that Trump gave Harp a $45,000 holiday cash gift. Two other aides, Margo Martin and Chamberlain Harris, also reported $45,000 gifts, while Walt Nauta reported a $20,000 gift. Harp's government salary is $150,000, meaning the payment represented roughly 30% of her annual salary.When Harp accompanied Trump on his Ireland trip, independent journalist Aaron Rupar posted a photograph and wrote: "Look who made the trip to Ireland!", using his recurring #TravelWithNatalie hashtag. The White House's Rapid Response 47 account responded by calling Rupar a "sick, deluded freak" and accusing him of posting "creepy" material.2. The mysterious kidney disease appearing among young Texas workersA form of chronic kidney disease that has devastated agricultural workers in parts of Central America and South Asia is now drawing attention in Texas, after doctors encountered cases among relatively young workers without the usual risk factors associated with kidney disease.The condition is generally called chronic kidney disease of unknown etiology, or CKDu. It is also known by names including Mesoamerican nephropathy and chronic kidney disease of nontraditional cause.Ordinary chronic kidney disease is strongly associated with conditions such as diabetes and high blood pressure. CKDu has repeatedly been documented among people who do not have those conventional explanations. Research has particularly focused on young agricultural workers doing physically demanding work in very hot environments.Researchers have proposed several possible explanations: prolonged heat stress, dehydration, agrochemicals, contaminated water, heavy metals and other environmental exposures. There is still no single universally accepted explanation for the disease. A 2025 review of more than 150 publications concluded that the cause remains unresolved, although occupational heat stress and dehydration are among the leading areas of investigation.3. Object between Saturn and Uranus is changing ringsThe object is called 10199 Chariklo, and it is not a planet or even one of the Solar System's major asteroids. It belongs to a relatively unusual class of small bodies called Centaurs, which orbit in the region between the giant planets. Chariklo is only about 250 km (155 miles) across. Yet it has something that, until relatively recently, astronomers associated primarily with giant planets: rings.New observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), published September 9 in Science Advances, indicate that Chariklo's two rings have changed significantly since astronomers first studied them. The inner ring appears to have become more opaque, while the outer ring has become much less apparent in the new observations.Chariklo was discovered in 1997. It became famous in 2013, when astronomers studying it through a phenomenon known as a stellar occultation discovered that it was surrounded by two narrow, dense rings."By comparing JWST observations with those obtained … over the last decade, we discovered opposite changes in the two rings: while the inner ring shows significantly higher opacity, the outer ring shows lower opacity, " Pablo Santos-Sanz, a researcher at the Institute of Astrophysics of Andalusia and first author of the study, said in a statement.4. Sauerkraut and JD Vance's weight loss secretAt a White House press briefing on September 3, a reporter asked Vance about his noticeable weight loss and, rather unexpectedly, asked how much sauerkraut he ate.Vance responded with a story about Lent.He said that on Fat Tuesday he had considered giving up sugar and social media. He then called Robert F. Kennedy Jr., whom he described as being particularly interested in health. Kennedy advised him to do something more intense and talked about eating a high-protein diet and "a lot of sauerkraut." Vance joked that if that was Fat Tuesday, "Fat Wednesday never came."It was an odd political-media moment: the vice-president of the United States discussing fermented cabbage at a White House briefing.Robert F Kenndy Jr made sauerkraut popular in the Trump cabinet though a few weeks earlier Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he was not among the converts and he could not carry his fridge containing jars of fermented cabbage everywhere he traveled.Sauerkraut itself is a particularly revealing example of how immigrant culture disappears into what later generations regard as ordinary American life. The Library of Congress notes that German immigrants were among the major forces shaping 19th-century American culture, with sauerkraut among the distinctly German contributions that became part of American life.5. The Cat in the Hat "killer" that wasn't In August, social media users in Britain and Ireland began circulating photographs and videos allegedly showing a sinister figure dressed as the Cat in the Hat stalking streets at night.The character was recognisable not simply as Dr Seuss's creation, but as the version played by Mike Myers in the 2003 film.But there was no killer. It was all AI.The images and videos were part of a social-media hoax, with AI-generated material mixed with staged footage and real people in costumes. Police in Britain and Ireland warned people about the misinformation.US schools and police departments began warning about posts using the Cat in the Hat imagery to threaten schools, communities and specific individuals. Several teenagers were arrested or charged in connection with posts associated with the trend. In one Connecticut case reported this week, a student was arrested over a threatening social-media post involving the character.The original book, published in 1957, was part of a major transformation in American children's publishing. It became an enormous commercial success and helped establish Dr Seuss as a central figure in the development of modern children's books and early-reader publishing.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Meet Myreen Ahsan, the Friendswood 8th-grader who screened over 10 million drug-like molecules with AI for a frontotemporal dementia project
articles.summary: US News: An eighth-grade student from Texas has used artificial intelligence and computer models to screen more than 10 million drug-like molecules in search o.
articles.body: An eighth-grade student from Texas has used artificial intelligence and computer models to screen more than 10 million drug-like molecules in search of possible treatments for frontotemporal dementia. Myreen Ahsan, a student at Friendswood Junior High in Friendswood, Texas, carried out the computer-based study as part of an independent research project on neurodegenerative diseases. Her project examined large chemical databases to find compounds that could interact with specific biological targets linked to the condition. The project earned Ahsan a place as one of 30 national finalists in the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge, a major science and engineering competition for American middle school students run by Society for Science. Frontotemporal dementia is a group of brain disorders that mainly affect the frontal and temporal parts of the brain. The condition can cause changes in behaviour, language, and the ability to plan and make decisions. Effective treatments that can slow or change the course of the disease remain limited, leading researchers to explore new ways to discover drugs.High-throughput virtual screening processAhsan named her research project "Millions to Molecules: Dual Mechanism Small-Molecule Discovery via HTVS and Machine Learning-Guided Molecular Dynamics for Frontotemporal Dementia". The study used high-throughput virtual screening (HTVS), a computer-based method that allows scientists to test large collections of chemical structures against biological targets digitally. This can reduce the time and cost involved in physically testing millions of substances in laboratories. Ahsan combined virtual screening with machine learning models and molecular dynamics simulations. This approach allowed her to study how strongly potential drug molecules might bind to target proteins and how stable those interactions could remain over time. Through several filtering steps, her computer-based process reduced the original library of more than 10 million possible molecules to a small group of promising small-molecule candidates. According to research summaries released by the Science and Engineering Fair of Houston, where Ahsan had previously competed, her approach focused on finding small molecules that could potentially work through two different mechanisms. The goal was to address more than one disease-related process at the same time.Self-taught computational techniquesAhsan became interested in medical computing through independent learning and by attending specialised neuroscience camps. Speaking about her research at an earlier symposium, Ahsan explained how advanced bioinformatics tools first caught her attention. "While preparing for my science fair project, I came across an article on AlphaFold 3.0 and its role in drug discovery. It felt like two worlds I was passionate about, AI and neuroscience, suddenly clicked together," Ahsan said. She taught herself how to use complex bioinformatics platforms and datasets by reading scientific research and studying public online resources. "It started with curiosity," Ahsan explained. "I treated it like a puzzle. I kept learning bit by bit until it made sense. It wasn't always easy, but it was exciting and that made the hard parts worth it." Her use of advanced data methods drew attention from academic experts during state and regional presentations.Xiaoqian Jiang, chair of the Department of Health Data Science and AI at UTHealth Houston, praised Ahsan's interest in advanced medical technology after one of her research presentations. "To see a young person so deeply engaged with cutting-edge topics demonstrates the extraordinary potential of the next generation," Jiang said. "Her work not only reflects a strong understanding of artificial intelligence in biomedical sciences but also showcases her curiosity and commitment to learning."National competition in WashingtonAhsan's selection among the top 30 finalists in the Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge followed a nationwide process that began with thousands of middle school students taking part in local and regional science fairs. After being nominated through the Science and Engineering Fair of Houston, Ahsan was named to the top 300 shortlist announced by Society for Science. She later secured a place among the 30 national finalists. As a finalist, Ahsan will travel to Washington, DC, for the competition's Finals Week. During the event, students will present their individual projects and take part in team-based problem-solving challenges judged by panels of scientists and engineers. Each finalist receives a $500 cash prize. The top awards at the national competition include more than $100,000 in educational scholarships and prizes. The finalists are scheduled to present their completed research projects to judges and the public during the Washington event in late October.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: As missing figures rise, kin of Nepal flood victims seek law change for death certs
articles.summary: Rest of World News: New Delhi: Relatives of people missing in Nepal’s devastating Aug 26 floods are pressing govt for a fast-track legal mechanism to have them declared d.
articles.body: New Delhi: Relatives of people missing in Nepal’s devastating Aug 26 floods are pressing govt for a fast-track legal mechanism to have them declared dead, saying absence of bodies and death certificates has blocked compensation, insurance claims, bank access, inheritance and property transfers. The demand gained urgency after authorities revised the number of missing from 5,179 to 6,150, while Nepal’s death toll stood at 1,403, with only 158 bodies identified.Some families, having lost hope of finding their relatives alive, have already performed symbolic last rites using effigies made of kusha grass where bodies were never recovered. But legally they remain in limbo, unable to obtain death certificates required for relief payments and other financial settlements.Prem Pokharel, whose younger brother Durga Prasad disappeared while working at the immigration office in Timure, said he had almost given up hope. “He hasn’t been found. I don’t believe he is alive,” Pokharel told TOI.Sabitri Tamang of Nuwakot said the legal deadlock had also stopped families from receiving money needed for funeral rites. After approaching her ward office for assistance, she was told nothing could be released without a death certificate.Nepal’s Civil Code generally allows a person continuously missing for 12 years to be presumed dead, but section 40(4) provides a separate route for relatives to seek a judicial declaration of death when someone disappears or is believed to have died in a disaster or accident. Courts can make such a declaration even without recovery of a body if sufficient evidence establishes the circumstances.Families and local officials, however, say forcing thousands of flood-hit households to separately approach courts, collect documents, produce witnesses and establish the circumstances of disappearance would create another costly and lengthy ordeal.Uttargaya rural municipality chief administrative officer Jayaram Upreti said ward offices currently lacked authority to issue death-related documents where no body had been recovered and identified.Nuwakot chief district officer Shambhu Prasad Regmi acknowledged the uncertainty confronting families and said authorities had discussed extending facilities available to families of the deceased to those whose relatives remained missing.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Meet Arjun Jain, the 16-year-old New Jersey student who turned a backyard hydroponics hobby into a project that has grown and distributed 3,500+ pounds of produce and helped shape two local ordinances
articles.summary: US News: A 16-year-old student from New Jersey has turned a backyard soil-free farming experiment into an urban agriculture project that has donated more than .
articles.body: A 16-year-old student from New Jersey has turned a backyard soil-free farming experiment into an urban agriculture project that has donated more than 3,500 pounds of fresh produce to local food pantries while also helping shape local laws. Arjun Jain, a student from Holmdel, New Jersey, started experimenting with hydroponics in his backyard after seeing how food insecurity affected nearby communities. Hydroponics allows plants to grow in water filled with nutrients instead of traditional soil. It can use much less water and land than standard farming. What began as a small personal project soon grew into a nonprofit organisation called HydroProduce. Through the initiative, Jain installed automated hydroponic growing systems in community spaces, school gardens and local facilities. The systems have produced thousands of pounds of fresh vegetables for families in need across Monmouth and Middlesex counties. According to a profile published by Action for Nature, an international environmental organisation that named Jain a 2024 International Young Eco-Hero, the project has provided fresh, nutrient-rich greens to food banks that often have difficulty keeping fresh vegetables available.Expanding access to fresh greensTraditional food banks often depend on canned and other shelf-stable foods because fresh produce can spoil quickly and requires more storage space. Jain designed his hydroponic systems to provide a regular, year-round supply of leafy greens, tomatoes and herbs directly to distribution centres. By building small, vertical hydroponic units, his team showed that large amounts of vegetables could be grown indoors or in small outdoor spaces without the need for large farmland. The project gained support in local communities, leading Jain to work with schools and civic groups. He held workshops to teach young people and residents how to build low-cost hydroponic systems with easily available materials. The workshops also helped families learn how to grow some of their own food at home. His work attracted the attention of environmental groups and local government officials across New Jersey. The project showed how small-scale technology could help address food shortages in communities with limited access to fresh produce.Shaping local municipal lawsJain's work also moved beyond growing food and into local policy. As his urban farming projects grew, he found that local zoning rules did not always cover newer forms of soil-free farming. Many municipal planning rules in suburban New Jersey did not clearly address vertical farms, indoor growing structures or community hydroponic systems on residential or public property. After identifying these gaps, Jain worked with local officials and planning boards to help develop clear rules for soil-free farming. His research, data collection and advocacy contributed to the drafting and approval of two local ordinances in New Jersey. The new rules created clear legal guidelines for residents and community groups that wanted to operate hydroponic and vertical farming systems. By reducing administrative barriers, the updated laws made it easier for schools, community centres and neighbourhood groups to establish local food-growing systems. Action for Nature highlighted this policy work in its awards documentation, saying Jain's work with municipal councils showed how young environmental advocates can contribute to long-term policy changes while also working directly in their communities.International recognition for youth advocacyThe impact of the HydroProduce project earned Jain international recognition through the 2024 International Young Eco-Hero Awards. Action for Nature gives the annual awards to young people aged 8 to 16 who carry out their own environmental projects and create measurable benefits for their communities. A panel of judges, including environmental scientists and educators, selected Jain based on the project's environmental benefits, community impact and policy work. Jain has also worked to share his hydroponic designs internationally. He created simple, open-source plans for hydroponic units that could be used in areas with limited resources. The designs are intended to help communities facing water shortages or poor soil conditions. Jain continues to expand HydroProduce while attending school. His current work includes installing more growing systems in local schools and working with regional food rescue organisations to increase the amount of produce the project can provide each week.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: GTA 6 album: Soundtrack reveal revives digital release debate
articles.summary: Fred Again, PinkPantheress and Travis Scott provide new music for the blockbuster - but not all fans are happy.
articles.body:
The reveal of a Grand Theft Auto 6 soundtrack album has reignited a debate over the decision not to release the game on disc.

Developer Rockstar Games announced a 34-track compilation, set to release on CD and vinyl on the same day as the highly anticipated video game.

The company says it will include original music from a "genre-defying roster of the most exciting artists in the world" including rapper Travis Scott, country singer Morgan Wallen and UK singer PinkPantheress.

But some fans have pointed out the "irony" of putting out a physical edition of the album following its controversial decision for a digital-only release of the game.

The first six tracks, published at the time of the announcement, also include rapper Yung Lean, British DJ Fred Again and Rolling Stone Keith Richards.

GTA games feature multiple radio stations, usually themed around a particular musical genre, which players can switch between while driving.

In the past the game's soundtracks have largely been made up of licensed music from established artists, although original songs have also featured.

Rockstar has said the upcoming game will feature a "dynamic score" and "evolution of in-game radio".

Being included in a Grand Theft Auto game can bring a new generation of fans to an artist's music.

Spotify streams of Tom Petty's Love is a Long Road, the track used in GTA 6's first trailer, increased by 36,979% after the clip was published.

Hot Together, by the Pointer Sisters, also saw a huge jump when it soundtracked the game's second trailer.

And a collection of tracks used in the recent Extended Look attracted new listeners in the week after it premiered on Netflix.

According to music and gaming publication MusicEXP , pop duo Captain & Tennille's 1980 track But I Think It's a Dream saw the biggest spike, jumping from 70 Spotify streams in one week to 80,744.

Cliff Richard's Devil Woman was streamed more than one million times, while Prefab Sprout's Cars and Girls jumped from 49K to 187K additional weekly streams.

It also noted increases in activity on music detection app Shazam around tracks featured in the 26-minute broadcast.

Some artists have refused to let Rockstar use their music in GTA games.

Martyn Ware, from synth pop band Heaven 17, called the developer out on social media, accusing them of offering a "pitiful" deal to use 1983 hit Temptation .

Grand Theft Audio? The tricky business of music and gaming

What we know after the big Grand Theft Auto 6 preview

GTA 6 is expected to be one of the biggest entertainment releases of all time when it comes out on 19 November.

The previous game in the series, GTA 5, broke records when it came out in 2013 and has sold more than 200 million copies since.

Two official trailers for the sixth game have almost 500 million combined views on YouTube, and the Netflix "extended look" reportedly topped the streamer's charts, despite a string of leaks in the lead-up to its release .

The company is currently involved in an employment tribunal in Scotland to defend itself against claims it illegally sacked a group of ex-employees for trying to form a union.

It strongly denies the accusations, and says the workers were fired on the grounds of gross misconduct.

articles.title: In 2024, Australian couple bought a 1,840-sq-m block to live next door to family; two years later, council says two modular homes make an ‘estate’, leaving them paying rent and mortgage on a home they can’t build
articles.summary: Rest of World News: The dream of staying close to family remains a pipe dream for an Australian couple. In 2024, Caitlin Holme and Chris Robinson bought into a sprawling .
articles.body: The dream of staying close to family remains a pipe dream for an Australian couple. In 2024, Caitlin Holme and Chris Robinson bought into a sprawling 1,840-square-metre block in Bulli, hoping to build a second modular home. Ms Holme's sister already occupied one on the rear of the property. Their plan was simple: two families, two homes and a shared block. The sisters could live next door. But it has been two years, and the couple is still waiting to build their home. What’s the problem? According to Wollongong City Council, two modular homes on the property constitute a ‘manufactured housing estate’, which is not allowed under the site’s zoning rules.No home, and yet paying mortgage and rent"I think not many people realise there was this weird thing. Like suddenly two houses means it's a manufactured housing estate? It's not a caravan park,” Ms Holme told ABC News. The city council’s decision has left the couple, who are raising two young children, without a home while still paying rent and a mortgage."We don't want to give up on the plan of living next door to my sister and her family; it's too good of a dream to walk away from at the moment. The reality is housing prices are more expensive and our generation has to be a bit more creative about how you make that a reality. But I think [with] everything we've been through in this process, we're not super optimistic anymore; we still just feel so up in the air,” she told the broadcaster.When two homes become an ‘estate’The couple wanted to be close to their family, so they bought into the 1,840-sq-m block in 2024. Ms Holme's sister was already living in the modular home at the back of the property. The couple planned to build their modular home at the front. They were about to live their dream life. "It felt like an amazing way we could live in a beautiful spot and make it easier in terms of costs. This idea was planted when I was pregnant with our first child, who is now four... now we've got our second, and she's just turned one,” Ms Holme said.The timing stings because Holme and Robinson were following the NSW government's own playbook. State and federal policy actively encourages modular construction as a solution to the housing crisis. In May, the government announced plans to change building laws, citing the Productivity Commission’s estimate that modern construction methods could reduce building costs by up to 20% and cut construction times by half. The couple was confident that their application would be approved, as the same modular home builder had already completed similar dual-occupancy projects in other parts of NSW, including Port Stephens. Instead, their application was rejected.Wollongong City Council said putting two modular homes on the site fell within the definition of a ‘manufactured housing estate’. "The Wollongong Local Environment Plan permits one such modern method of construction (MMC) development per allotment within the current zoning," a spokesperson said."More than one MMC home presently constitutes a manufactured housing estate, which is not permissible under the current zoning. Planning legislation does not allow a council to approve a prohibited use."More troubleThe couple wanted to find a way to make this work. After all, they were still paying rent and a mortgage without actually being able to live in their new home. So they consulted a town planner, subdivided the land and resubmitted their application. But the outcome was the same."It feels like we're still in purgatory. I feel like we did everything that was asked of us. We followed the state and federal government's advice to move out of the city. They're spruiking modular housing. We ticked all those boxes and now we're just waiting,” Mr Robinson told the network.Proposed reforms could change the processThe NSW government has since introduced building reforms intended to remove the distinction between modular and traditionally constructed homes in the approvals process. Building Minister Anoulack Chanthivong said the changes would establish a single approval pathway for all housing, regardless of construction method. "It will establish a new building approvals pathway that will no longer be determined by the construction method, so a house will be treated as a house whether it be prefabricated, traditionally built or a combination of both," the minister said in a statement. The minister added that the reforms would cut red tape, speed up approvals and make it easier to build homes. The city council also stated that it had asked for clearer legislation for approving modular builds."Further detail is required and [the] council is looking forward to the new legislation clarifying definitions and planning pathways that will better enable us to consider modular housing applications. This includes vagaries within the definitions and requirements for manufactured homes and manufactured home estates,” a spokesperson said.Planning Minister Paul Scully was more direct about the inconsistency and said the proposed reforms would resolve the family’s trouble. "When you've got this anomaly… that modern methods of construction aren't dealt with in the same way as traditional methods of construction, we've got to deal with that. If we pass the bill… that uncertainty gets resolved."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Stafford tower block arsonist jailed for setting woman alight
articles.summary: Reece Brivitt is jailed after dousing the woman in petrol and vodka before setting her alight.
articles.body:
A man who set a woman on fire inside a flat, after dousing her in petrol and vodka, has been jailed for 11 years and nine months.

Reece Brivitt, 33, set the victim alight inside a tower block flat on Milton Grove, Stafford, on 22 October.

The victim suffered serious burns to her chest and legs, leaving her with life-changing injuries, the court heard.

Brivitt admitted charges of arson with intent to endanger life as well as wounding with intent and was sentenced at Stafford Crown Court on Wednesday.

Brivitt was also served with an indefinite restraining order against the victim.

Det Con Jessica Scott, of Staffordshire Police, said the arsonist had "subjected his victim to a cruel attack, which has left her with life-changing injuries".

"The incident not only threatened the life of the victim, but of all those who were in the flats at the time," she added.

The swift actions of firefighters meant the fire was extinguished quickly, preventing further injuries, she explained.

Delivery group manager Mark Walchester, from Staffordshire Fire and Rescue Service, said: "Crews worked quickly to minimise the risk posed to those in the flat block during this incident and to ensure the fire was extinguished as quickly as possible.

"Fires in flat blocks and houses of multiple occupancy have the potential to devastate lives."

articles.title: How Uttarakhand construction workers can avail Rs 50,000 house loan with minimal interest rate
articles.summary: News News: For construction workers, arranging the finances needed to purchase or build a house can be a significant challenge. To provide financial support for .
articles.body: For construction workers, arranging the finances needed to purchase or build a house can be a significant challenge. To provide financial support for this purpose, the Uttarakhand government offers assistance to eligible registered construction workers through a loan at a minimal interest rate. The financial assistance for purchase or construction of house scheme is implemented by the Uttarakhand building and other construction workers welfare board (UKBOCWWB) under the Labour Department, government of Uttarakhand.Under the scheme, registered construction workers can receive an advance loan of up to Rs 50,000 for the purchase or construction of a house, subject to the conditions specified by the Board. The loan carries an interest rate of at least 5 per cent per annum.Eligibility and documents requiredIn order to avail the benefit, the applicant must be a construction worker registered with the UKBOCWWB.To avail the advance loan, the worker must have been a member of the fund for at least five years and must have at least 15 years remaining until the superannuation or retirement age.The application must be accompanied by the following documents:Shramik CardAadhaar CardBank account detailsA handwritten self-declaration certificate stating that no assistance has been taken from any other department for the same purpose.Application processThe application process is online, submitted through shramik suvidha kendras. After submission, the application is subject to departmental verification and investigation.If the application is found to be correct during the verification process, the advance amount is disbursed. The worker is required to pay interest per annum on the advance.Proof of completion of the work must be submitted to the secretary of the Board within six months from the date of withdrawal of the advance. The sanctioned advance amount is recovered in equal instalments as determined by the Board.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Los Angeles NBC helicopter seen plummeting toward ground in dashcam video
articles.summary: Dashcam video captures the NBC and Telemundo 52 helicopter's rapid descent over Los Angeles before the fiery crash that killed three people.
articles.body: Dashcam video from a Los Angeles driver captured an NBC and Telemundo news helicopter rapidly descending toward the ground moments before a fiery crash that killed three people. The video, captured by driver Year Valencia, shows the helicopter dropping from the sky Tuesday while its crew was covering a separate deadly collision involving an SUV and a city bus. "I downloaded the video of my dashcam. It’s a little dot on the video. It’s a crisp video, and it just goes down," Valencia told KTLA, which first obtained the footage. "God, it’s so close, it could have happened to anyone. My parents walk down the street." NBC REPORTER, PILOT AMONG THE VICTIMS IDENTIFIED IN DEADLY LOS ANGELES HELICOPTER CRASH The helicopter crashed in the Chatsworth neighborhood of the San Fernando Valley, killing NBC4 and Telemundo 52 reporter Eliana Moreno, pilot George Marciniw and 29-year-old Edy Gutierrez Mejia, who was on the ground. The aircraft went down near a storage facility and caught fire, with the blaze spreading to at least four vehicles and two storage containers. The crash came roughly two hours after the SUV slammed into the city bus in a separate collision that killed two people and injured six others, according to authorities. Police said the SUV had been traveling the wrong way, ran a red light and struck another vehicle before hitting the bus. VICTIMS IDENTIFIED IN FATAL AMAZON CARGO JET CRASH AT MIAMI AIRPORT Police arrested the SUV's driver, 36-year-old Bailee Lynn Rios, on murder charges Tuesday night. The Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office was reviewing the case to determine what charges, if any, would be filed in court. The cause of the helicopter crash remained under investigation Wednesday. Video broadcast from the helicopter before it went down captured an alarm sounding inside the aircraft as it began losing altitude. National Transportation Safety Board investigator Fabian Salazar said Wednesday that the helicopter's final video could provide investigators with critical evidence as they work to determine what caused the crash. The sounds captured on the recording appeared consistent with changes in engine speed and likely cockpit advisory tones, he said. The NTSB is investigating the helicopter crash as well as the earlier bus collision.

articles.title: Hyrox athlete apologises for continuing race after soiling herself
articles.summary: Joanna Wietrzyk has also forfeited her win in the fitness competition after competing last week.
articles.body:
An Australian athlete who faced criticism for continuing to compete in a Hyrox event after soiling herself has apologised and said she will retroactively withdraw from the race.

Joanna Wietrzyk offered her "sincere apology" for the incident during the indoor fitness competition in Beijing on Saturday, saying she should have "made a different choice" and exited the event.

Footage of Wietrzyk competing after soiling herself raised concerns about hygiene, leading Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste to apologise for the handling of the situation.

In a statement shared on Thursday, Wietrzyk said: "I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected."

Hyrox apologises for allowing race to continue after athlete soils herself

How Hyrox became the latest sporting craze

After the backlash, Wietrzyk, who won the race in Beijing, said she would forfeit her win.

Wietrzyk said in a social media post: "I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the HYROX organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing."

She wrote in a social media post that she was "completely fit and healthy" at the start of the race, and had "no reason" to expect any illness.

"Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognize that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused," Wietrzyk continued.

Hyrox insisted it had "clear biocontaminant and medical procedures in place".

It said "an unforeseen situation arose" during which protocols became blurred, "creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood".

In a statement posted on Instagram, Fürste committed to "improving event processes" to "prevent situations like this from happening again".

After Wietrzyk's identity was shared online, Hyrox said anyone sending abuse or threats to the athlete would be banned from any future events.

It said on Monday: "There is no place in our community for threats of violence or encouragement to harm an athlete."

In each Hyrox race, participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises, including a sled push, burpee jumps, indoor rowing, and lunges while carrying a sandbag.

The competition has exploded in popularity since it was founded in 2017 in Hamburg, Germany, and is now held across the world. The sport debuted in mainland China in late 2024.

Some have questioned why those officiating the competition in Beijing last weekend did not intervene when the athlete soiled herself, given that Hyrox penalises acts including "spitting, nostril clearing, littering, and water abuse".

articles.title: What could EU associate member status mean for Canada?
articles.summary: Mark Carney says he is seeking a "unique" relationship with the bloc, but currently there is no such thing as an associate member.
articles.body:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has welcomed the European Union's ambition to make his country the first associate member of the bloc – but what would that mean in practice?

Carney says he is seeking a "unique" relationship with the EU, in an apparent reference to the fact that EU treaties do not currently provide for associate membership.

Germany had proposed Ukrainian associate membership earlier this year but Kyiv rejected the idea, saying it only wanted full EU integration. The EU itself also seemed reluctant.

But EU chief Ursula von der Leyen has now shifted the focus across the Atlantic to Canada

At the her State of the Union address on Wednesday, von der Leyen listed several key areas for cooperation, although she did not give specific details about how Canadian associate membership would work.

What Carney says about EU associate membership

Carney told reporters on Thursday that Canada was "not in a position, nor seeking, to become a full member of the European Union".

He also said it was not an attempt to create a "third bloc", adding: "We do not seek power to dominate others."

He told the European Parliament on Thursday that closer alignment between Ottawa and the EU was needed to confront the "current geopolitical rupture" – nodding to strained relations with the US following President Donald Trump's tariff policy and the collapse of trade talks between the two countries.

At the European Parliament on Thursday, Carney set out what he views as key areas where his country and the EU can cooperate, including:

Carney also said he wanted to move towards membership of the EU's Erasmus Plus scheme – the funding programme which allows students to work and study abroad. All 27 EU states are members and there are seven non-EU members. The UK will rejoin the scheme in 2027.

He said Canada could contribute liquefied natural gas (LNG) and hydrogen "at large scale to support Europe's energy security" and that Canada in turn could benefit from what he described as Europe's leadership on clean energy technologies.

What could associate membership look like?

So we know what it is not – full membership of the EU.

It is not clear is what exactly the relationship would look like. EU associate membership does not currently exist and the process to create it could take years.

If associate status were enshrined in EU treaties, it would require unanimity and ratification among all 27 member states.

Despite von der Leyen's overtures towards Canada, some EU countries would prefer to build on existing defence and trade agreements rather than create a new form of membership.

The EU is Canada's second-largest trading partner and the far-reaching Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement was agreed more than a decade ago, though several of the bloc's 27 members are yet to ratify that agreement.

The current trade deal does not remove border checks. Would associate membership change that?

It also remains to be seen what associate membership would mean for Canada's relationship with the European single market.

Were Canada to one day join the single market, it would have to match EU regulations and standards while having no say on policy – in a similar way to European Economic Area countries Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein, or Switzerland, which has a separate deal.

Canada's rules have historically been geared towards its biggest trade partner, the US.

And then there's the matter of other countries seeking to join the bloc.

Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia and Serbia are already on the long road towards full EU membership, while in Eastern Europe, Georgia and Moldova are also pursuing membership.

There is no suggestion that a new relationship with Canada would hinder these countries' progress towards full accession, but any impression that Ottawa was being given special treatment could create tension.

There is also the question of Trump's response. He has described the prospect of Canada's associate membership as "laughable" and has threatened further tariffs on the EU if the plan goes ahead.

articles.title: As missing figures rise, kin of Nepal flood victims seek law change for death certificates
articles.summary: South Asia News: Relatives of people missing in Nepal’s devastating Aug 26 floods are pressing govt for a fast-track legal mechanism to have them declared dead, saying.
articles.body: Relatives of people missing in Nepal’s devastating Aug 26 floods are pressing govt for a fast-track legal mechanism to have them declared dead, saying absence of bodies and death certificates has blocked compensation, insurance claims, bank access, inheritance and property transfers. The demand gained urgency after authorities revised the number of missing from 5,179 to 6,150, while Nepal’s death toll stood at 1,403, with only 158 bodies identified.Some families, having lost hope of finding their relatives alive, have already performed symbolic last rites using effigies made of kusha grass where bodies were never recovered. But legally they remain in limbo, unable to obtain death certificates required for relief payments and other financial settlements.Prem Pokharel, whose younger brother Durga Prasad disappeared while working at the immigration office in Timure, said he had almost given up hope. “He hasn’t been found. I don’t believe he is alive,” Pokharel told TOI.Sabitri Tamang of Nuwakot said the legal deadlock had also stopped families from receiving money needed for funeral rites. After approaching her ward office for assistance, she was told nothing could be released without a death certificate.Nepal’s Civil Code generally allows a person continuously missing for 12 years to be presumed dead, but section 40(4) provides a separate route for relatives to seek a judicial declaration of death when someone disappears or is believed to have died in a disaster or accident. Courts can make such a declaration even without recovery of a body if sufficient evidence establishes the circumstances.Families and local officials, however, say forcing thousands of flood-hit households to separately approach courts, collect documents, produce witnesses and establish the circumstances of disappearance would create another costly and lengthy ordeal.Uttargaya rural municipality chief administrative officer Jayaram Upreti said ward offices currently lacked authority to issue death-related documents where no body had been recovered and identified.Nuwakot chief district officer Shambhu Prasad Regmi acknowledged the uncertainty confronting families and said authorities had discussed extending facilities available to families of the deceased to those whose relatives remained missing.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: Elon Musk's mother Maye Musk said Elon always wanted to do good for others even when he was a child, but his approach often put him at odds with others. Maye opened up about her personal journey in an interview with CBS Mornings co-host Gayle King on her new memoir "Timeless". Maye said Elon Musk was a genius child and he ""just wants to do good in the world, but that means you stand on a lot of toes." She said she believes he's been treated unfairly by members of the public."People are mean. And they're strangers, or they're not accomplished themselves, and then they can do insults," she said. "It makes me angry."She said she wants people to know, "He does whatever is best for America and what's best for the world," adding, "And then, if we don't listen, then let's go to Mars."Her comments come after a turbulent period for Elon Musk, whose brief stint in the US government as the head of the Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, drew considerable criticism. DOGE overhauled federal agencies and cut funding for several programmes during the early months of President Donald Trump’s second term.Musk later had a public falling-out with Trump after leaving the administration, including criticism of Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill”. The relationship has since appeared to improve. Musk has also backed Republican candidates in the 2026 midterm elections. Meanwhile, his business empire has continued to expand. SpaceX went public, making Musk the world's first trillionaire.When Gayle King asked Maye Musk whether she agreed that Elon was on the spectrum as a child, Maye said: "Well, when I read 'the spectrum,' maybe on one of the points that he's a little awkward, yeah."In her memoir, Maye recounted her struggle in an abusive marriage and how she moved from South Africa to Canada with her three children, where she started her own practice as a dietitian. "I didn't know it was possible," she said. "Until you just have enough, and you run away."Maye said her children did not complain when she was juggling parenting and her studies for her first master's degree and when they all had to sleep on couches and floors. "I said to them, 'Why did you put up with that?' And they said, 'Well, if we complained, would you listen?' And I said 'No,'" Musk recalled.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Jalen Hurts saw Philadelphia schools closing because they had no AC; after funding 300+ units, he is now giving $600,000 to the city's largest high school
articles.summary: US News: Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts has pledged $600,000 to install air conditioning units at Northeast High School, expanding his ongoing eff.
articles.body: Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts has pledged $600,000 to install air conditioning units at Northeast High School, expanding his ongoing effort to help keep local students in classrooms during periods of extreme heat. The donation is aimed at the city's largest public high school, which serves more than 3,300 students. According to The Philadelphia Inquirer, the money will pay for the purchase and installation of commercial-grade cooling units to help control temperatures across the large campus. For years, extreme heat in early autumn and late spring has forced the School District of Philadelphia to dismiss students early or cancel classes because of poor climate control in older school buildings. Hurts began his cooling initiative after seeing how rising temperatures in the city were repeatedly disrupting classes at public schools.Building on earlier pledgesThe Northeast High School pledge represents a major increase in Hurts' financial support for local school infrastructure. In April 2024, Hurts pledged $200,000 through the Jalen Hurts Foundation to provide air conditioning systems for 10 Philadelphia public schools. That funding paid for more than 300 air conditioning units and helped improve indoor conditions at selected schools across the district. The latest $600,000 commitment is focused on Northeast High School, where the size and age of the building have created major heating and cooling challenges. Staff and students gathered at the school when Hurts personally announced the pledge. Photos published by The Philadelphia Inquirer showed the NFL player speaking to students and school officials inside the building, which has experienced repeated disruptions during periods of hot weather. School district officials said the investment will address long-standing equipment shortages that have made it difficult for staff to keep classrooms at safe temperatures.Widespread infrastructure challengesThe funding for Northeast High School also highlights wider problems with school infrastructure in Philadelphia and other cities across the United States. Many Philadelphia public schools were built decades ago, before air conditioning became common in school buildings. According to information from the School District of Philadelphia, dozens of school buildings do not have central air conditioning, leaving them more affected by rising seasonal temperatures. When indoor temperatures become too high, district officials may order early dismissals to help protect students and teachers from heat-related illness. These unexpected closures can create problems for working families who must quickly find childcare or change their work schedules. During previous heat events, representatives of the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers have repeatedly called for more investment to update school buildings and cooling systems. The school district has a multi-billion-dollar capital improvement plan, but limited funding has slowed HVAC upgrades across more than 200 district-operated properties.Community impact and player philanthropyHurts' donation comes as professional athletes increasingly use charitable giving to address specific problems in their local communities instead of supporting only general programmes. By focusing directly on classroom cooling, the foundation aims to reduce lost class time caused by extreme temperatures. Local educators welcomed the investment, saying comfortable classroom conditions can affect students' concentration, attendance and ability to learn during hot weather. With installation plans underway, district technicians expect the new equipment to be ready before future periods of hot weather that could otherwise disrupt the school schedule.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Only 25 scimitar-horned oryx returned to Chad in 2016 after vanishing from the wild, but the population has now grown to more than 600
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 2016, just 25 scimitar-horned oryx were flown from Abu Dhabi to Chad, marking the first time the species had set foot in the wild since it vanished.
articles.body: In 2016, just 25 scimitar-horned oryx were flown from Abu Dhabi to Chad, marking the first time the species had set foot in the wild since it vanished there in the 1980s. Since then, according to Sahara Conservation and the Environment Agency, Abu Dhabi, 285 oryx have been released into Chad's Ouadi Rimé-Ouadi Achim Faunal Reserve, and the wild population has grown past 600 animals, prompting the IUCN to downlist the species from Extinct in the Wild to Endangered.How the scimitar-horned oryx vanished from wild AfricaThe scimitar-horned oryx, a desert antelope once widespread across North Africa, was declared Extinct in the Wild by the IUCN in 2000 after decades of overhunting and habitat loss stripped it from its native range. The last wild sighting in Chad came in the late 1980s. Surviving animals existed only in zoos and private collections worldwide, so the Environment Agency, Abu Dhabi, built a genetically diverse "World Herd" from more than 220 institutions to supply future reintroductions. In 2016, the first 25 oryx were flown from Abu Dhabi to Chad, landing at Abéché airport before being released into the Ouadi Rimé-Ouadi Achim Faunal Reserve.Inside the scimitar-horned oryx reintroduction program in ChadThe Scimitar-Horned Oryx Reintroduction Project launched in 2014, led by the Environment Agency, Abu Dhabi, in partnership with the Government of Chad and Sahara Conservation, with support from the Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute, the Zoological Society of London, Saint Louis Zoo, and others. The first oryx calf born in the wild arrived in December 2016, just months after release. According to the Abu Dhabi Media Office, From that initial group of 25, the program went on to translocate 285 scimitar-horned oryx into Chad's reserve over the following years, using satellite collars and field monitoring to track survival, movement, and reproduction across the herd.Why Chad's oryx population passed 600 and its status improvedBy 2023, more than 500 calves had been born to the reintroduced oryx in the wild, pushing the total wild population past 600 individuals, well beyond the project's original target of 500 animals. On 11 December 2023, the IUCN reclassified the scimitar-horned oryx from Extinct in the Wild to Endangered, a milestone for one of the most ambitious large-mammal conservation programs ever undertaken. Officials noted that one released female had given birth to nine calves since 2016, and that the overall survival rate for reintroduced oryx in the wild now exceeds 85 per cent.What the oryx's recovery means for Chad's wider ecosystemThe oryx's recovery has had knock-on benefits for the wider Ouadi Rimé-Ouadi Achim Faunal Reserve, one of the largest protected areas in the world, where the project has expanded to support addax, dama gazelle, and North African ostrich populations as well. Sahara Conservation continues to oversee day-to-day management of the release site, while the Government of Chad enforces wildlife protections across the reserve. Officials from Sahara Conservation and its partners have said the milestone shows that species written off as extinct in the wild can still be restored through sustained international collaboration, though continued monitoring remains essential to the population's long-term survival.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Europe, Canada are stronger together’: Carney after Trump calls EU ‘associate member’ proposal ‘laughable’
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday backed closer ties between Canada and the European Union, saying the two sides could work together to .
articles.body: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday backed closer ties between Canada and the European Union, saying the two sides could work together to protect their markets, democracies and sovereignty, hours after US President Donald Trump called the proposal “laughable” and threatened to impose tariffs on Europe.Addressing the European Parliament in Strasbourg, Carney welcomed the EU’s ambition to make Canada its first “associate member”, although he did not himself use the term.“Europe and Canada are each strong. Europe and Canada are even stronger together,” Carney was quoted as saying by news agency Reuters.Carney did not name Trump in his speech but appeared to refer to US trade measures, saying economic integration was being “weaponized” through tariffs and that supply chains and financial mechanisms could be used for coercion.Trump threatens tariffs on EuropeTrump on Wednesday criticised the proposal to deepen EU-Canada ties, calling the idea of Canada becoming an associate member of the bloc “laughable”. He also threatened to impose “very heavy tariffs” on Europe or stop trading with the bloc on some goods if he considered the move a “hostile act”.“If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe,” Trump told reporters in North Carolina.The remarks came after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed on Wednesday that the EU should open the door for Canada to become its first associate member.The proposed status does not currently exist under EU treaties and would need to be created and approved by the bloc’s member states.The European Commission said the proposal was not directed against the United States. “The proposed strengthening of our partnership with Canada is not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” Commission spokesperson Olof Gill said.Carney: No one can dictate Canada’s choicesCarney said the final structure of any future relationship with the EU would be decided through discussions and would ultimately require a vote in the Canadian Parliament.“Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak. No one is going to dictate our culture or with whom we can strike agreements internationally,” Carney told reporters after his speech.He said Canada was looking at closer cooperation with Europe in areas including critical minerals, defence, artificial intelligence and computing, energy security, space and payments.Carney also stressed that Canada and Europe were not seeking to create a rival power bloc. “I’m not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great power rival, only with better manners,” he said.The EU and Canada already have a free trade agreement, the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), which provisionally came into force in 2017 and eliminated 99 per cent of tariff lines.The proposed closer partnership comes as Canada and the US remain locked in a trade dispute, with Washington having increased tariffs on Canadian goods and Ottawa responding with tariffs of its own.French Europe Minister Benjamin Haddad said on Thursday that the US could not veto the EU’s geopolitical decisions. “It is not up to the United States — or anyone else — to choose the political and geopolitical direction of the Europeans,” he said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A tech entrepreneur bought a ruined Welsh island fort for £500,000, but after £2 million and a decade of work it became an 8,000-sq-ft off-grid home
articles.summary: UK News: In 2017, British tech entrepreneur Mike Conner bought Thorne Island, a ruined 19th-century fort off the coast of Pembrokeshire in Wales, for about £50.
articles.body: In 2017, British tech entrepreneur Mike Conner bought Thorne Island, a ruined 19th-century fort off the coast of Pembrokeshire in Wales, for about £500,000 after seeing a video about the property online. At the time, the island had no electricity or running water and the fort had been left in a derelict condition after earlier attempts to revive it as a hotel failed. Conner, the former chief executive of software company Appsbroker, subsequently embarked on an extensive restoration of the Victorian fort, investing around £2 million in the project. The result is a property with more than 8,000 square feet of accommodation, five bedrooms and enough space to sleep up to 20 guests. The restored island has solar panels, battery storage, heat pumps and other infrastructure that allows it to operate independently of mainland utilities. In August 2025, Conner put Thorne Island on the market for £3 million through Strutt & Parker.The military history of Thorne Island fort off the coast of PembrokeshireThorne Island sits at the entrance to Milford Haven, a strategically important waterway leading towards the former Royal Dockyard at Pembroke Dock. The fort was constructed between 1852 and 1854 as Britain expanded its coastal defences amid concerns about the growing strength of the French Navy under Emperor Napoleon III. It formed part of the wider group of Victorian coastal fortifications associated with Lord Palmerston's defence programme.The fort was designed to accommodate a garrison of about 100 men and featured a seaward-facing artillery battery. Its original armament included five seven-inch Armstrong guns and four 68-pounder guns, mounted in open positions behind the parapet. The landward side contained the defensible barracks, while the fort's thick walls provided protection for the garrison and artillery. Thorne Island's military role eventually ended, and in 1947 the fort was converted into a hotel. The property subsequently changed hands several times. It was sold for £275,000 in 1999, and in 2001 the Von Essen hotel group acquired the island with plans for a £4 million five-star hotel and a cable car linking it with the mainland. Those plans did not materialise. The island was sold again in 2011 and was put back on the market in 2016 before Conner acquired it the following year.How Mike Conner restored the ruined fort into an off-grid island homeConner's restoration involved far more than renovating the interiors. When he bought the island, the fort lacked basic utilities and had suffered years of exposure to moisture. The isolated location also meant that construction materials and equipment had to be transported from the mainland by helicopter or boat. Contemporary reports say hundreds of helicopter trips were required during the restoration, while builders lived on the island for several years as work progressed.The restoration included extensive work to the historic granite structure, as well as the installation of modern water, heating, sewage and electrical systems. Reports have put the overall investment at around £2 million, with a substantial portion devoted to renewable-energy and infrastructure systems. These include solar panels, battery storage and heat pumps, while a dedicated sewage system and water-treatment infrastructure allow the island to function without conventional mainland utilities. Conner has described the project as a personal challenge undertaken after his career in technology. He bought the island after seeing it advertised as a derelict property and spent years turning the former military installation into a functioning private retreat. The restoration retained much of the original character of the fort, including exposed masonry, vaulted ceilings and the historic layout, while incorporating modern living spaces.What the restored Thorne Island fort offers today for £3 millionThe finished property now contains just over 8,000 square feet of accommodation spread through the restored fort. The current sale listing describes five bedrooms, an open-plan kitchen and snug, large reception and dining areas, a games room and a rooftop bar. Several rooms retain exposed traditional brickwork and vaulted ceilings, while large windows provide views across the surrounding waters. The island also comes with its own private jetty and helipad, allowing access by boat or air. A hydraulic crane is used to move supplies and equipment between boats and the island, an important feature given that Thorne has no conventional road connection to the mainland. The property is being marketed for private residential use as well as potential commercial or hospitality purposes.Thorne Island covers about 2.5 acres and the fort is a Grade II* listed building. Its location also places it within the wider Pembrokeshire coastal landscape, with the surrounding waters forming part of an area known for marine wildlife and historic shipwrecks. The island itself has therefore retained both its military heritage and its unusual position at the entrance to Milford Haven. After years spent turning a derelict Victorian fort into a functioning private retreat, Conner put Thorne Island on the market in 2025 for £3 million. The sale listing presents the property as a rare combination of historic architecture, private-island access and modern off-grid infrastructure, while leaving its next use open to whoever takes on the unusual Welsh property.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Johnny Marr guitars sell for more than £560k at auction
articles.summary: One instrument was used on the The Smiths' debut album and also appeared on the cover of Oasis's debut single.
articles.body:
Two guitars owned by Manchester musician Johnny Marr have sold for more than £560,000 at auction.

The instruments, which were used during his time with The Smiths and on his forthcoming solo album, went under the hammer as part of Christie's Marr's Guitars: The Johnny Marr Collection sale.

Marr's 1982 Rickenbacker 330 Jetglo sold for £358,400 after attracting a bidding battle lasting more than five minutes.

The guitar was used throughout the recording of The Smiths' debut album and on the band's early tours. It can be heard on songs including This Charming Man, Still Ill and What Difference Does It Make? The instrument also featured on the cover of Oasis's debut single Supersonic.

Marr had lent it to Noel Gallagher during early recording sessions for Oasis' album Definitely Maybe.

A second guitar, Marr's 1960 Cherry Red Gibson ES-355, sold for £204,800.

The instrument inspired him to write the music for The Smiths' 1984 single Heaven Knows I'm Miserable Now and its B-side Girl Afraid.

It was bought for him in 1983 by Sire Records founder Seymour Stein after Marr joked that The Smiths would sign to the label if he bought him a new guitar.

The auction comes ahead of the release of Marr's first studio album in four years, The Age Of Everything, which is due out on 2 October.

Marr was guitarist and co-songwriter for The Smiths alongside singer Morrissey.

The Manchester band released four studio albums before splitting in 1987 and became one of the defining groups of the British indie music scene.

The 111-lot auction is continuing, with further items expected to sell for thousands.

articles.title: Scarborough's 'AI slop' art trail cost £11,688, figures reveal
articles.summary: Artists and residents in Scarborough criticised the trail when it was launched in the summer.
articles.body:
An art trail created by an agency using computer-generated designs described by one artist as "AI slop" cost £11,688, a Freedom of Information request has revealed.

The Giant Deckchair Trail was commissioned by North Yorkshire Council as part of Scarborough's 400th anniversary celebrations, with each of the 10 deckchairs depicting a moment in the seaside town's history.

Dozens of artists and residents in the resort previously said they were "deeply disappointed" by the authority's decision to use AI.

However, the council said the trail had made a "positive contribution" to the anniversary.

According to the Local Democracy Reporting Service , the authority declined to detail any other costs involved in the project and would not name the agency which undertook the work.

The council said that due to the "significant media attention and substantial hostile online commentary", the suppliers had told the authority "disclosure of its identity in connection with the current controversy would be likely to result in significant commercial prejudice and adversely affect future commercial business opportunities".

Several quotes had been sought for the project, although "the cost of the design was below the procurement threshold that requires three quotations", the council said.

It added that two North Yorkshire-based design agencies and two artists were initially selected and three proposals were received in response, "with one agency selected upon review of the proposals".

Adrian Riley, a Scarborough-based artist who designed the mural on the side of the Central Tramway Station and on the front of the town's railway station, described the deckchair designs as "AI slop".

"We're a tourism destination and an important part of that is people visiting for culture," he said.

"You can get AI anywhere in the world, but you can only visit the workshops, galleries, exhibitions and studios of many local artists by actually being here in Scarborough."

When the deckchair trail was revealed this summer, artist and illustrator Hannah Grahamslaw said: "It's not just the impact on my own employment that offends me, my concerns are mainly that all AI 'art' is stolen from artwork created by real artists.

"It is is damaging to the environment. It takes jobs from artists, without whom North Yorkshire would be an extremely dull and grey place."

Tony Watson, North Yorkshire Council's head of economy and tourism, said the trail had been a successful part of the town's anniversary celebrations.

It had provided a "free, family-friendly attraction that encouraged residents and visitors to explore different areas of Scarborough throughout the summer", he said.

The trail had generated more than 14,000 QR code scans and had high engagement and attracted "positive feedback from participants and host venues as well as considerable social media interest", Watson said.

He added that the authority had held constructive discussions with local artists who had expressed concerns about the role of AI in the design process.

"While we believe its use was justified in this instance, we will continue to consider such technology on a case-by-case basis."

articles.title: Saudi Arabia facing 'biggest threat' ever to oil production as Iran-proxy Houthis launch attacks, expert says
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia faces the biggest threat to its oil production since 1932 as Houthis launch attacks near the Red Sea's Bab el-Mandeb Strait, an expert says.
articles.body: Saudi Arabia is currently facing "the biggest threat" ever to its production of oil as the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen are launching cross-border attacks and seizing territory near the Red Sea’s Bab el-Mandeb Strait, an expert told Fox News Digital. Hussain Abdul-Hussain, a research fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said Thursday that the situation is escalating in the Middle East as Iran "likely instigated the Houthis to force a blockade on Saudi Arabia." "I think this situation is really precarious for the Saudis. This is the biggest threat to their production of oil since their kingdom was founded in 1932. And this is almost existential," he said. "We see that the Saudis are trying to shop for some force to fight their war for them. And I think along the lines, they also called President Trump. It doesn't look to me that Washington is going to get involved in this one," he added. "We'll probably offer them advice and tell support, but I don't think we, the United States, will get involved with this war over Bab el-Mandeb." IRAN-BACKED TERROR GROUP'S LATEST TERRITORIAL GRAB THREATENS SECOND GLOBAL SHIPPING CHOKEPOINT Saudi Arabia was forced to temporarily close its East-West oil pipeline last week following a drone attack launched from Iraq, which Trump said he believes Iran was behind. Then on Tuesday, Saudi Arabia destroyed a Houthi drone that attempted to enter the airspace near Mecca, among other recent provocations. "We know that the United States imposes a blockade on Iran, so Iran is unable to export any of its oil, licitly or illicitly. What the Iranians are trying to do is that they're trying to telegraph to the other oil exporters in the region that either we export, all of us export oil, or none of us will export oil," Abdul-Hussain told Fox News Digital. "This is why you see Iran shutting down the Strait of Hormuz. This forced Saudi Arabia to switch its oil production from east to west, from Hormuz to the other side to the Red Sea. Tankers started picking up oil at the port of Yanbu in Saudi Arabia on the Red Sea and sailing south through the Bab al-Mandeb all the way to the Asian markets. "Iran didn't like this because clearly all or none didn't work," he said. "So they likely instigated the Houthis to force a blockade on Saudi Arabia." HOUTHIS ENTER US 'KILL BOX' AFTER SEIZING RED SEA ISLAND, FORMER PENTAGON OFFICIAL WARNS Fox News Digital, citing a source familiar with the matter, reported on Friday that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman urged Trump to take military action against the Houthis. Trump then said the next day during a visit to Ireland that "the Houthis called us and they don’t want to fight with us." "They let us know, they don’t want to fight with us...they don’t want us to go after them," Trump added. "But they have called and they have talked to us, and they don’t want us to, they would much prefer not having us involved." Abdul-Hussain told Fox News Digital that "Our expectation as Washington is that the Saudis, with all these arms that we've sold them over the past few decades, with all the military support and advice we give them, that they should be able to protect their own tankers and ships in this waterway and keep it open. "The Houthis announced that they're only going after Saudi ships and Saudi navigation and they made it clear that they are not going after international shipping, whether [they] are U.S. ships or European ships," he continued. "So this forces a choice on us. Do we go to war with the Houthis out of nowhere, even though they're not willing to, or at least they didn't wage war on our ships and our navigations through Bab el-Mandeb?" "Or we ask the Saudis to handle this, you know, after all the Houthis are not really a state, they're a non-state actor and Saudi Arabia should be able to deal with them," Abdul-Hussain added. "Unfortunately, the Saudis don't seem to have been able to deal with the Houthis." articles.title: Dumfries flood scheme request approach criticised by watchdog
articles.summary: Dumfries and Galloway Council "failed at the most basic level" in its response on the Whitesands project.
articles.body:
A council "failed at the most basic level" in its response to freedom of information (FOI) requests about a flood protection scheme, a watchdog has found.

Dumfries and Galloway Council was asked about common good land affected by the Whitesands project and whether it had petitioned the courts for a change of use.

It initially claimed the information was exempt but, after an appeal to the Scottish Information Commissioner (SIC), said it did not hold it at all.

However, when asked what searches had been carried out, it said there had been none as it had "no reason to believe the information should be held". The council is now considering the commissioner's findings.

Work begins on Dumfries flood defence scheme

The street that has flooded more than 200 times

The £68m Whitesands flood protection scheme has been a contentious one.

Campaigners have called for it to be dropped due to its rising cost, visual impact and loss of car parking spaces.

However, work began this year to protect an area which has been flooded hundreds of times since records began.

Two FOIs were submitted to the council by a member of the public about the impact on common good land - owned by the council for the benefit of the community - and whether it had petitioned the courts for a change of use.

SIC David Hamilton has delivered a highly critical verdict on how they were handled.

"It is a simple and fundamental principle of FOI that public bodies first conduct a full and appropriate search for information covered by a request, before then considering whether that information can be disclosed," he said.

"The council's approach here, however, was entirely wrong-headed, turning this important principle upside down.

"It first said that its legal advice was exempt from disclosure, before then going on to claim that it wasn't held - despite having not carried out any searches for it."

He said that was "entirely unacceptable".

"I will not tolerate attempts to cut corners or shut down requests when it comes to the exercise of information rights," he said.

"I will be watching carefully to see whether this was an unfortunate isolated incident, or whether it is symptomatic of a wider issue that requires more direct action."

The council will now be required to carry out detailed searches to identify if it does hold the information requested.

The SIC can also take further action "where there is evidence that repeated failures are occurring".

A council statement said: "We have only today received the SIC's decisions and are currently considering their findings and requirements.

"We will fully consider and respond within the timescales set out.

"It would be inappropriate to comment further until we have had an opportunity to review the decisions in detail."

Town's £68m flood scheme cleared to progress
